result: The Drosophila pupal ecdysis sequence occurs at the onset of metamorphosis and consists of three principal phases (P1, P2, P3) characterized by distinct motor programs that always proceed in the same order. These movements increase internal pressure to evert the head and elongate developing appendages.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C18-C22 provide a well-established description of the pupal ecdysis sequence based on prior work and current observations. The temporal placement, phase structure, and functional outcomes are clearly documented with both textual descriptions and figure references (Figure 1A-C). This represents established background knowledge that frames the study.

result: Approximately half of larval muscles persist until pupal ecdysis, with the most prominent loss occurring in ventral and posterior compartments. This pattern was consistent across 17 animals, indicating pupal ecdysis is executed by a standard set of persistent larval muscles.
evaluation: Claims C23-C32 describe anatomical characterization of pupal musculature based on phalloidin labeling (Figure 1D-G) with adequate sample size (N=17). The specific muscle counts and distribution patterns are clearly documented with both imaging data and supplementary information. The conclusion that a standard muscle set executes pupal ecdysis is well-supported by the consistency across animals.

result: A new pan-muscle LexA driver (hlk-LexA) was generated from the hulk gene that permits imaging of muscle Ca++ activity through the clarified puparium. This tool successfully reports known pupal ecdysis behaviors and differentiates the three behavioral phases.
evaluation: Claims C33-C39 describe the development and validation of a key methodological tool. The genetic construction is clearly described (C35-C36), and validation is demonstrated by showing that observed muscle activity patterns match known behaviors (C38) and differentiate phases P1-P3 (C39, Figure 2). This represents a well-supported technical advance that enables the subsequent analyses.

result: Ca++ imaging revealed a previously undescribed Phase 0 (P0) of random muscle activity beginning approximately 3 hours before P1, characterized by distinct bouts of small muscle contractions that coincide with body wall twitches rather than coherent movements.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 describe the discovery of P0 with clear temporal placement (C47), characterization of activity patterns (C48), and quantitative measurements of muscle length changes (C49, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The distinction from coordinated movements is well-documented. This represents a novel finding enabled by the improved imaging methods.

result: Dual imaging of synaptic and muscle activity during P0 shows that synaptic Ca++ activity at the NMJ precedes muscle responses by 30-40 minutes, with coincident activity increasing progressively until P1 onset when nearly all muscles (except M12) and their synaptic inputs are synchronously active.
evaluation: Claims C51-C54 describe dual-channel imaging results (Figure 3B-D) showing the temporal relationship between synaptic input and muscle response. The specific timing (30-40 min), progressive increase in coincidence, and exception of M12 are clearly documented. This provides strong evidence that P0 activity is neurogenic rather than myogenic.

result: Class I dendritic arbor neurons that act as proprioceptors during larval locomotion persist at the pupal stage and show correlated Ca++ activity with muscles during P0. Suppression of these neurons with Kir2.1 causes sustained, widely distributed Ca++ activity before twitching stops, and all animals (n=10) died before P1.
evaluation: Claims C55-C60 combine anatomical observation (C56, Figure 3E), functional correlation (C57-C58, Figure 3F-G), and genetic manipulation (C59-C60, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The lethality finding is unexpected but clearly documented with adequate sample size (n=10). The results suggest proprioceptive feedback is essential for pupal ecdysis initiation, though the mechanism of lethality requires further investigation.

result: Five canonical movements were defined using muscle activity patterns and body wall displacements, including the Swing, Brace, Crunch, Anterior Compression, Posterior Contraction, and Posterior Swing. A precise onset for P3 was defined based on the Crunch movement.
evaluation: Claims C61-C73 describe detailed characterization of individual movements with clear criteria based on muscle activity patterns and anatomical compartments (Figure 4A, Video 5, Table 1). The descriptions include temporal relationships (C64-C67), spatial organization (C66, C70), and phase specificity (C73). The definition of P3 onset addresses a previous difficulty in the field (C62).

result: A convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained to recognize and annotate the defined movements.
evaluation: Claim C74 describes the development of an automated analysis tool (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). The CNN training and validation are documented, though detailed performance metrics are in supplementary materials. This represents a methodological advance that enables systematic analysis across animals.

result: The pupal ecdysis sequence shows relative stereotypy at the level of bulk Ca++ traces, but variation exists in bout durations, interbout intervals, and bout numbers. Coefficients of variation were lowest for P2, suggesting it is the most tightly regulated phase. Movement order showed considerable stereotypy with mean sequence similarity scores above 0.6 for all phases.
evaluation: Claims C75-C83 provide quantitative analysis of behavioral variability at multiple levels (Figure 5, Supplementary file 2). The use of sequence similarity scores and coefficients of variation provides objective measures. The interpretation that P2 is most tightly regulated (C79) is supported by the CV data (C78). Sample sizes appear adequate (N=10-16 animals depending on analysis).

result: The order of muscle activation in P1 bouts yielded a sequence similarity score of 0.44 ± 0.17, which differed significantly from shuffled sequences (0.32 ± 0.12, p<0.001), indicating the sequences are not entirely random despite low similarity.
evaluation: Claims C84-C86 provide statistical analysis comparing observed muscle activation sequences to shuffled controls. The significant difference (p<0.001) supports the conclusion that sequences are not entirely random (C86), though the low similarity score (0.44) indicates substantial variability. The statistical approach is appropriate.

result: Eight co-active muscle groups called 'pupal muscle ensembles' (PMEs) were identified based on specific criteria. Muscles forming a PME are not recruited in a consistent order. Together with individual movement-associated muscles, these are collectively termed 'syllables'.
evaluation: Claims C87-C90 describe the identification of PMEs using clearly defined criteria (Figure 6D, Table 1). The finding that PME muscles are not recruited in consistent order (C88, Figure 6C) is important for understanding motor variability. The syllable concept provides a useful framework for analyzing motor organization at an intermediate level between individual muscles and whole movements.

result: Syllable recruitment order was quite variable (sequence similarity scores below 0.5), but P2 and P3 syllable sequences were significantly more consistent than individual muscle sequences. P1 syllable sequences showed similarity to muscle sequences, suggesting random muscle activations outside syllables may contribute to P1 movements. Idiosyncratic muscle activations were common in all phases.
evaluation: Claims C91-C95 provide comparative analysis of sequence stereotypy at muscle vs. syllable levels (Figure 6E). The finding that syllables provide more consistent sequences in P2/P3 but not P1 (C92-C93) reveals phase-specific differences in motor organization. The documentation of idiosyncratic activations (C95, Figure 6F) is important for understanding the limits of stereotypy.

result: Stereotypy for ordered motor execution in pupal ecdysis is highest for phases and incrementally decreases with spatiotemporal scale. The least stereotypy (sequence similarity <40%, CV >40%) is seen in individual muscle recruitment order, which is less consistent than syllable activation.
evaluation: Claims C96-C100 synthesize the multi-level analysis of behavioral stereotypy (comparing Figures 6E and 5D). The hierarchical organization of stereotypy—highest at phase level, decreasing through movements, syllables, to individual muscles—represents a key conceptual finding. The specific quantitative thresholds (C99) are clearly stated.

result: P1 bouts initiate in the posterior compartment with syllable activation in A6 driving the Lift. Ventral syllables activate first, followed by prolonged dorsal activity of PME4 (M1-3), together compressing posterior segments. In anterior segments, compression is transient with coincident dorsal and ventral activity, while lateral transverse muscle contraction pulls the dorsal surface away from the puparium.
evaluation: Claims C101-C107 provide detailed spatiotemporal analysis of P1 movements (Figure 7D). The descriptions of compartment-specific activation patterns and their mechanical consequences are well-supported by the imaging data. The speculation about reduced surface tension (C107) is appropriately qualified as 'may be facilitated'.

result: Syllable activation in P2 bouts is considerably more uniform across hemisegments, body axes, and time compared to P1. Syllables from all dorsoventral compartments activate together in each hemisegment, with a wave of compressions traversing the body wall in the posterior-to-anterior direction.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 describe the distinct spatiotemporal organization of P2 compared to P1 (Figure 7E). The increased uniformity and coordinated activation across compartments are clearly documented. The P-to-A wave is demonstrated by delayed activation in A4 relative to A6.

result: Fluorescence increases moderately correlated with muscle shortening (r = -0.54). During P2, M12 and muscles of PMEs 1-4 shorten the most. Greatest D-V constriction occurs in posterior segments, while longitudinal compression is greater anteriorly, consistent with the absence of M12 posteriorly and greater dorsal muscle shortening anteriorly.
evaluation: Claims C111-C116 provide quantitative analysis of muscle mechanics during P2 (Figure 8A-C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A). The moderate correlation between fluorescence and shortening (C111) is important for interpreting Ca++ signals. The spatial patterns of shortening and their relationship to muscle distribution are well-documented.

result: Peak Ca++ activity of PME2 muscles increases from A5 to A3, opposite to the trend in muscle shortening, meaning these muscles work harder to generate smaller length changes in anterior segments. This suggests counterforces on the anterior body wall consistent with increased pressure to evert the head.
evaluation: Claims C117-C119 provide important mechanical insight by comparing Ca++ activity and muscle shortening (Figure 8A vs. 8B). The interpretation of increased work against counterforces (C118-C119) is reasonable and supported by citation to previous pressure measurements in blowflies. This represents a key functional insight.

result: Each Swing is initiated posteriorly when hemolymph is uniformly distributed and pressure is low. Ascending compression pushes the opposite body wall against the puparium, driving hemolymph forward to create anterior pressure maintained by isometric contractions. The unilateral Swing extrudes larval tracheal linings deposited on the puparium.
evaluation: Claims C120-C125 provide a mechanical model of Swing function (Figure 8E-F). While some aspects are inferential (C120-C123), they are based on observed muscle activity patterns and body wall movements. The tracheal extrusion function (C124-C125) is directly documented by imaging (Figure 8F). The model integrates multiple observations into a coherent functional explanation.

result: The Lift and RollCon movements of P1 share features with the Swing and likely prepare the animal for P2. The Lift uses bilateral contraction of similar syllables as the Swing, while RollCons engage only a subset of syllables with smaller muscle changes and lack M12 activity. The active elements of P1 appear to merge in P2 into one robust P-to-A movement.
evaluation: Claims C126-C135 provide comparative analysis of P1 movements relative to P2 (Table 1, Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The quantitative differences in muscle activity (C131) and the functional explanations for why RollCons only deflect while Swings compact (C134) are well-supported. The synthesis that P1 elements merge in P2 (C135) is a reasonable interpretation.

result: In P3, coordinated movement separates into multiple compartmentalized movements without strictly repeating units. Bulk Ca++ activity shows an initial variable pattern evolving into alternating wide peaks and double peaks. The Crunch heralds the variable period, followed by various combinations of Brace, AntComp, PostCon, and PostSwing that form fairly regular repeating blocks with some variation.
evaluation: Claims C136-C152 provide detailed characterization of P3 organization (Figure 2C, Figure 8—figure supplement 2). The description of movement blocks and their evolution is well-documented. The speculation about increased pressure driving hemolymph into appendages (C152) is appropriately qualified as 'may' and supported by imaging of leg extension.

result: Suppressing NETHRB neurons disrupts P1 initiation by blocking abdominal lifting and severely attenuates baseline muscle Ca++ increase. Although some P1-characteristic PMEs appear, activity in M15/M1 (PME4) is missing, PME1 muscles don't exhibit ensemble activity, and D-V compartments are not synchronized in posterior segments. This indicates ETH-targeted neurons coordinate muscles into syllables to produce the lift movement.
evaluation: Claims C153-C162 describe genetic manipulation results with clear phenotypic characterization (Figure 9A-D, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A). The sample size (N=6) is adequate for the observed effects. The conclusion that NETHRB neurons coordinate syllable formation (C160) is well-supported by the specific deficits observed. The persistence of deficits in later movements (C161-C162) is also documented.

result: Suppressing CCAP-secreting neurons results in normal P0 and P1 activity but absent P2 and P3. A single partial swing-like movement occurs after numerous P1 bouts, but PME4 fails to form correctly, the P-to-A wave is disrupted, the partial swing propagates only through A5, and PME2 is unsynchronized with longitudinal muscles. NCCAP modulates generalized muscle activity increase, syllable coordination along A-P axis, and activity coordination across D-V axis.
evaluation: Claims C163-C176 provide comprehensive characterization of NCCAP suppression effects (Figure 9E-F, Figure 9—figure supplement 1B-D, Video 6). Sample size (N=10) is adequate. The quantitative measurements of reduced fluorescence and length changes (C170) support the conclusions. The multi-level deficits (generalized activity, A-P coordination, D-V coordination) are well-documented and lead to clear conclusions about NCCAP function.

result: CCAP-R-expressing motor neurons innervate approximately half of pupal muscles via Ib synapses, including all dorsal and three ventral muscles, but none of the lateral transverse motor neurons express CCAP-R. However, the transverse muscles M21-23 of PME2 are labeled by CCAP-R-Gal4, suggesting CCAP centrally modulates motor neuron output to dorsal/ventral muscles while directly modulating lateral transverse muscles.
evaluation: Claims C177-C181 describe anatomical characterization using Split Gal4 intersectional labeling (Figure 10A-C, Supplementary file 1). The pattern of expression is clearly documented. The interpretation of dual central and peripheral modulation (C181) is reasonable given the expression pattern, though it remains inferential without functional validation.

result: At the larval stage, CCAP is co-released with Bursicon from type III terminals on M12 and M13. These terminals persist at the pupal stage, and M21-23 are responsive to bath-applied CCAP. The results demonstrate a role for NCCAP in coordinating syllable activity across A-P and D-V axes and a peripheral role for CCAP in directly modulating lateral muscles.
evaluation: Claims C182-C186 combine anatomical (C182-C183, Figure 10B) and functional evidence (C184, Figure 10D-E, Video 7). The persistence of type III terminals is documented by anti-Bursicon staining. The CCAP responsiveness is demonstrated in fillet preparations with appropriate controls (vehicle, Ca++-free media). The conclusions about dual central and peripheral roles (C185-C186) integrate multiple lines of evidence.

result: Suppressing Bursicon-expressing neurons has effects similar to NCCAP suppression: normal P1 but incorrect P2/P3 execution, lethality without head eversion, and a single swing-like movement consisting of an entire anteriorly directed wave. Some P3-like movements are observed but activity lacks organization and remains desynchronized in D-V compartments. D-V synchronization and sustained swinging require NBurs, while full A-P coordination additionally requires non-Bursicon-expressing neurons in NCCAP.
evaluation: Claims C187-C196 describe NBurs suppression effects (Figure 11A-C). Sample size (N=10) is adequate. The phenotype is similar to but distinct from NCCAP suppression, with the key difference being that a complete anteriorly directed wave occurs (C190) and some P3-like movements are detected by CNN (C191). The conclusions about differential requirements for D-V vs. A-P coordination (C194-C196) are well-supported by comparing the two manipulations.

result: The results of suppressing neuromodulatory signaling support both central and peripheral roles for ecdysis hormones in promoting syllable coordination across A-P and D-V axes. This coordination promotes behavioral coherence despite variable timing of individual muscle activation.
evaluation: Claims C197-C198 synthesize the neuromodulation results. The conclusion of dual central and peripheral roles is supported by the anatomical (CCAP-R expression) and functional (suppression phenotypes) data. The statement that coordination promotes coherence despite variability (C198) integrates the neuromodulation findings with the earlier variability analyses.

result: Hormonal signaling coordinates muscle activity across muscle ensembles and anatomical compartments to ensure stereotypy of behavioral execution. Stereotypy is evident at the phase level, but muscle recruitment into movements is not stereotyped and some muscle activity is not correlated with movement. Prior to ETH action, nervous system activity exhibits intrinsic variability that is reduced but not eliminated by neuromodulators, which incrementally increase behavioral coherence.
evaluation: Claims C199-C204 represent the main conclusions synthesized in the Discussion. These integrate the findings about hierarchical stereotypy (C200), uncorrelated activity (C201), P0 variability (C202), and neuromodulatory effects (C203-C204). The conclusions are well-supported by the collective evidence from variability analyses, syllable identification, and neuromodulation experiments.

result: ETH initiates pupal ecdysis after behavioral quiescence, targeting neurons expressing ETHRA and ETHRB receptors. ETHRB neurons are essential for pupal but not larval ecdysis. ETHRA neurons include CCAP and Bursicon-secreting cells that are essential at pupal ecdysis, become active ~10 min after onset, and mediate the transition to the next behavioral phase.
evaluation: Claims C3-C8 describe established background knowledge about hormonal control of pupal ecdysis, all supported by citations to previous work (Kim et al. 2006, Diao et al. 2016, Clark et al. 2008, Park et al. 2003). These provide essential context for the current study's neuromodulation experiments.

result: Using improved imaging methods including a new pan-muscle LexA driver, the authors identify novel elements of pupal ecdysis including a phase of stochastic muscle activity preceding ecdysis. Muscle activity exhibits high variability with muscles recruited stochastically into repeating small ensembles called syllables. Syllable activity is synchronized over anatomical compartments to form movements sufficiently stereotyped to be learned by a CNN. Suppressing neuromodulatory or proprioceptive neurons prevents synchronization and is lethal. Overall, movements are not rigidly specified but form from variable components subject to neuromodulatory reorganization.
evaluation: Claims C9-C17 represent the abstract/introduction summary of main findings. These are all supported by the detailed results described in other claim groups. This provides an accurate high-level summary of the study's contributions.

result: The alternating left-right oscillations of P1 persist through P2 and P3, with coordinated bilateral activity becoming dominant only in P3. Bulk Ca++ activity imaged from lateral side shows the same three phases. The Lift is performed by most muscles across the D-V axis in posterior segments, while RollCons typically lack activity in ventral longitudinal muscles 12, 13, and 15. P-to-A waves in P1 reverse direction after head eversion in P2.
evaluation: Claims C40-C45 describe validation of the hlk>GCaMP6s imaging system by showing it recapitulates known features of pupal ecdysis (Figure 2B-E, Videos 2-3). The consistency with previous work (Diao et al. 2017, Kim et al. 2006) and the detailed characterization of muscle activity patterns provide strong validation of the new tool.
